stem: After an overnight fast, an isolated liver is exposed to ethanol while receiving lactate and alanine. Glucose output falls, the lactate-to-pyruvate ratio rises, and the malate-to-oxaloacetate ratio rises. Which interpretation best explains the reduced gluconeogenic flux?
options: NADH shifts pyruvate to lactate and oxaloacetate to malate, depleting both glucose precursors
Ethanol permits acetyl-CoA to be converted back to pyruvate, which diverts carbon away from glucose production
Ethanol-derived NADH directly activates glucose-6-phosphatase, causing hepatic glucose-6-phosphate depletion
The increased lactate-to-pyruvate ratio shows that lactate dehydrogenase has stopped functioning
The increased malate-to-oxaloacetate ratio increases oxaloacetate availability for conversion to phosphoenolpyruvate
optionExplanations: ethanol oxidation raises hepatic NADH, shifting lactate dehydrogenase toward lactate and malate dehydrogenase toward malate, thereby lowering pyruvate and oxaloacetate available for gluconeogenesis.
human pyruvate dehydrogenase is irreversible; acetyl-CoA cannot be converted back to pyruvate and therefore cannot explain these redox-ratio changes.
glucose-6-phosphatase hydrolyzes glucose-6-phosphate in the ER and is not directly activated by NADH; the immediate ethanol effect is precursor depletion.
a high NADH level drives a functioning lactate dehydrogenase equilibrium toward lactate; the increased ratio does not indicate that the enzyme has stopped.
shifting oxaloacetate toward malate lowers, rather than raises, oxaloacetate available for PEP formation and thereby suppresses gluconeogenesis.
rationale: Ethanol oxidation raises the hepatic NADH-to-NAD+ ratio, pulling both pyruvate and oxaloacetate away from gluconeogenesis and toward lactate and malate.
sourceRef: Lippincott Illustrated Reviews: Biochemistry, 9th ed., Ch. 23 IV.C, alcohol-related hypoglycemia
missDescription: Selected acetyl-CoA to pyruvate instead of recognizing that ethanol-derived NADH shifts pyruvate to lactate.
variantAngle: Interpret paired hepatic redox ratios and precursor depletion instead of recalling a single reaction direction.

stem: A lymph-node biopsy shows selective loss of its delicate branching stromal mesh, while thick tensile bundles and elastic recoil are preserved. Loss of which matrix component best accounts for this pattern?
options: Type I collagen fibers
Elastic-fiber elastin
Elastic-fiber fibrillin
Type III collagen fibers
Adhesive glycoprotein fibronectin
optionExplanations: type I collagen forms strong, thick bundles; those bundles are described as preserved rather than being the lost branching stroma.
elastin provides stretch and recoil, and the stem explicitly states that elastic recoil remains intact.
fibrillin supports elastic-fiber microfibrils; preserved elastic recoil argues against selective loss of this component.
type III collagen forms reticular fibers, the fine branching mesh that supports mobile cells in lymphoid tissue.
fibronectin is an adhesive glycoprotein linking cells to matrix, not the principal protein of the branching reticular-fiber scaffold.
rationale: Reticular fibers are composed of type III collagen and form the delicate branching support network characteristic of lymphoid stroma.
missDescription: Selected type I collagen bundles instead of type III collagen reticular fibers for a branching lymph-node support network.
variantAngle: Infer fiber composition from a selective-loss biopsy pattern instead of choosing a fiber from its stated function.

stem: In a dermal explant, a treatment reduces radiolabeled proline incorporation into extracellular collagen and decreases secretion of ground-substance components. IgE-triggered mediator release and phagocytosis remain normal. Which connective-tissue cell was most likely inhibited?
options: Mast cell
Fibroblast
Monocyte-derived macrophage
White adipocyte
Plasma cell
optionExplanations: Mast cells use IgE receptors to release inflammatory mediators, and that function remains normal in the explant.
Fibroblasts synthesize collagen fibers and ground-substance components, matching both reduced matrix-production measurements.
Monocyte-derived macrophages phagocytose foreign material and dead cells, and the stem states that phagocytosis is preserved.
White adipocytes primarily store triacylglycerol in a large lipid droplet rather than producing the measured extracellular matrix.
Plasma cells synthesize immunoglobulin; they are not the resident cell responsible for collagen and ground-substance production.
rationale: The paired loss of collagen production and ground-substance secretion identifies fibroblast inhibition, while preserved mast-cell and macrophage functions exclude the closest immune-cell alternatives.
sourceRef: OST520 (026) L - Connective Tissue - Liang.pdf, cell-types section
missDescription: Selected mast-cell degranulation instead of fibroblast collagen and ground-substance secretion for a spindle-shaped wound-repair cell.
variantAngle: Infer cell identity from paired matrix-production assays with preserved immune-cell controls instead of inferring function from wound morphology and organelles.

stem: A normally soluble secretory protein has a hydrophobic sequence inserted midway through its polypeptide. Its N-terminal region enters the ER lumen, but a downstream reporter remains cytosolic and the protein stays membrane-associated. What role did the inserted sequence perform?
options: A second signal peptide restarted translocation of the downstream reporter into the ER lumen
An SRP-binding signal initiated the protein's first contact with the rough ER
A stop-transfer sequence halted translocation and became a membrane-spanning anchor
A signal-peptidase recognition site cleaved the protein free of the ER membrane
A translation-termination signal caused a release factor to end polypeptide synthesis
optionExplanations: A sequence that restarted translocation would place the downstream reporter in the ER lumen, opposite the observed cytosolic location.
The original N-terminal signal already initiated rough-ER targeting; the inserted internal segment instead determines later topology.
A hydrophobic stop-transfer sequence halts further passage through the translocon and exits laterally into the bilayer as a membrane span.
Signal peptidase cleaves an N-terminal signal in the ER lumen, whereas this internal segment remains in the bilayer as a membrane span.
Release factors recognize stop codons in mRNA, whereas the full downstream reporter was synthesized and remained cytosolic.
rationale: The inserted hydrophobic segment acted as a stop-transfer anchor: it halted lumenal translocation, entered the membrane laterally, and left the downstream region in the cytosol.
missDescription: Selected aminoacyl-tRNA binding instead of recognizing that a stop-transfer sequence creates a membrane-spanning domain.
variantAngle: Infer an inserted sequence's role from a topology experiment instead of predicting the structure lost after deletion, using new process-level distractors.

stem: A phagocyte has intact pentose-phosphate-pathway production of NADPH but no NADPH oxidase activity. Which reaction is most directly impaired when the cell encounters bacteria?
options: Reduction of oxidized glutathione to reduced glutathione
Production of ribose-5-phosphate for nucleotide synthesis
Conversion of fructose-6-phosphate to glycolytic intermediates
NADPH-dependent synthesis of nitric oxide
Transfer of electrons from NADPH to oxygen to form superoxide
optionExplanations: glutathione reduction uses NADPH through antioxidant machinery and can remain intact when the separate NADPH oxidase enzyme is absent.
ribose-5-phosphate production is a pentose-phosphate-pathway function and does not require phagocyte NADPH oxidase.
reversible carbon exchange between the pentose phosphate pathway and glycolysis does not depend on NADPH oxidase.
nitric oxide synthesis can use NADPH, but loss of NADPH oxidase specifically impairs the respiratory-burst reaction that begins with superoxide.
phagocyte NADPH oxidase initiates respiratory burst by transferring electrons from NADPH to molecular oxygen, producing superoxide.
rationale: NADPH oxidase uses PPP-derived reducing power to convert oxygen to superoxide at the start of the phagocyte respiratory burst, distinct from NADPH-supported antioxidant reactions.
missDescription: Selected glutathione instead of superoxide as the first NADPH-dependent product of phagocyte respiratory burst.
variantAngle: Infer the missing reaction from a selective enzyme defect while distinguishing pro-oxidant NADPH oxidase from glutathione recycling.

stem: Glucose carbon is incorporated into skeletal-muscle glycogen after a meal. During later exercise, the labeled carbon appears in muscle glucose-6-phosphate and lactate but not as free glucose released into blood. Absence of which muscle activity best explains this distribution?
options: Glycogenin-mediated priming of a new glycogen particle
Phosphoglucomutase interconversion of glucose-1-phosphate and glucose-6-phosphate
Glycogen phosphorylase cleavage at nonreducing alpha-1,4-linked ends
Glucose-6-phosphatase hydrolysis of glucose-6-phosphate in the ER
Glycogen synthase addition of glucose from UDP-glucose
optionExplanations: Glycogenin acts upstream by priming formation of a new glycogen particle; it does not dephosphorylate glucose-6-phosphate for export from muscle.
appearance of label in muscle glucose-6-phosphate requires phosphoglucomutase activity after glycogen-derived glucose-1-phosphate is formed.
mobilization of labeled glycogen carbon requires glycogen phosphorylase; its activity explains production of glucose-1-phosphate rather than failure to export glucose.
skeletal muscle lacks glucose-6-phosphatase, so glycogen-derived glucose-6-phosphate remains available for local glycolysis rather than becoming free blood glucose.
glycogen synthase is needed to store labeled glucose after the meal, but its presence or absence does not explain why mobilized carbon cannot be released as free glucose.
rationale: Muscle can synthesize and degrade glycogen and can form glucose-6-phosphate, but without glucose-6-phosphatase it cannot dephosphorylate that intermediate for blood-glucose export.
missDescription: Selected glycogenin instead of glucose-6-phosphatase as the reason muscle glycogen cannot directly maintain blood glucose.
variantAngle: Interpret tracer distribution across storage, local glycolysis, and blood export instead of recalling a tissue-specific enzyme absence directly.
